scenarios.name: single, lower income, no age threshold or phase-out exists so cases vary income instead of age
scenarios.source: Texas has no individual income tax and therefore no form to derive a figure from. Primary source: Texas Constitution, Article 8, Section 24-a, official text via the Texas Legislature's statutes site: 'Sec. 24-a. INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX PROHIBITED. The legislature may not impose a tax on the net incomes of individuals, including an individual's share of partnership and unincorporated association income. (Added Nov. 5, 2019.)' expectedStateTax = $0 follows directly from that constitutional prohibition, for any income composition. This case is a single filer with pension income only. No age threshold or AGI phase-out exists in Texas law (the prohibition is unconditional, not age-gated), so per the batch matrix rule this case and the next vary income rather than age.

scenarios.name: single, higher income including a Roth conversion, no age threshold or phase-out exists so cases vary income instead of age
scenarios.source: Same primary source as the prior case: Texas Constitution Art. 8 Sec. 24-a, 'The legislature may not impose a tax on the net incomes of individuals...' This case raises income well above the prior one and adds an IRA withdrawal and a Roth conversion, exactly the kind of income a multi-year conversion plan produces, to confirm the $0 result holds regardless of composition, not just for plain pension income.

scenarios.name: MFJ, both spouses present, moderate combined income including Social Security
scenarios.source: Same primary source: Texas Constitution Art. 8 Sec. 24-a. The prohibition applies to 'individuals' without reference to filing status, so it covers MFJ households identically. This is the MFJ 'both spouses qualifying' case in the batch matrix; because Texas has no age-gated exemption there is nothing to qualify for, so both spouses are simply present with retirement ages. Income mix adds taxable Social Security to the pension/IRA combination exercised in the single cases.

scenarios.name: MFJ, only one spouse retirement-aged, highest combined income in the batch
scenarios.source: Same primary source: Texas Constitution Art. 8 Sec. 24-a. This is the batch's 'MFJ, only one spouse qualifying' case; Texas has no per-spouse age gate for its (constitutionally prohibited) income tax, so there is no attribution rule to trip, but the case is included anyway per the matrix so a later phase adding an age gate has a case waiting. Highest income in the batch (pension + IRA withdrawal + Roth conversion) to stress the largest plausible single-year total against the $0 expectation.
